Hello everyone

I've fitted a Poisson GLM with a random intercept and a PC mattern spatial random effect to predict species richness for the US.

The model fits the data well, however, the posterior range of the spatial field is enormous (5000 km) and I can't find out, what exactly is the cause of it. Moreover, this is a larger value than the range that I've defined for the prior median range: 3200 (I chose 1/2 of the study area's extend as a very large starting point). My initial plan was to run it once with such a large posterior range to get a better Idea of the actual range - now I'm puzzled about the result and have trouble finding the cause of this unreasonable range.

So far I checked to reduce the prior range, gradually going down and approaching a range I would find meaningful, from the initial 3200 to 1000, 500, 400, 300, 200, 100. But the posterior range remained unchanged at around 5000. Furthermore, when lowering the median range to 100 or lower, I received the following error message:

5000 is quite similar to 3200, so for the run with 3200 as prior median, 5000 sounds perfectly reasonable...

But I wonder about your coordinates. What is the initial coordinate system/CRS? Your “conversion” seems to take raw long&lat values and divide by 1000, but long&lat aren’t in metres, they’re in degrees, so that conversion doesn’t seem to make sense. Also, setting units open a CRS only makes sense if that CRS knows about distance units, e.g. UTM.

Finn

5000 is quite similar to 3200, so for the run with 3200 as prior median, 5000 sounds perfectly reasonable...

range is a scale parameter like stdev, etc, so the error is relative,
(or thevariance of the parameter depends on the parameter), so to
quantify the error, its better to look at the ratio

range.estimated / range.true


and NOT

| range.estimated - range.true |

parts:
Just a short follow up, in case this rings a bell for anyone.

I am still unable to fully make sense of the output of my hyperparameters. But in another model I was able to resolve the issue with the range, but at the cost of having another hyperparameter with way of the normal range :

Meanwhile I've done the model selection for another response (inverse Simpson index) from the same data-set (same mesh, same prior median range, but slightly different sd for the SPDE and not a poisson, but gaussian model).
There, the best fitting model (f1 below) has the spatio-temporal term, too (like the best fitting model for species richness). But, judging by DIC & WAIC the best model for inverse Simpson included a temporal random effect and a temporal autocorrelated effect. In f1, the issue with the huge range that I had with the model for species richness is gone - I have a range which makes somewhat sense. However, now the precision of the for my temporal random term is extremely high.

Out of curiosity, I also made a model including the effects for the best model for species richness (f2 below) so this model contains only the effects of the model in the previous emails (spatio-temporal effect and iid effect) - there the huge range for the spatial random effect is suddenly back to what it was in the other model.

I find this odd, as I would not expect that adding another separable temporal term should be able to reduce the range of the spatial correlation so much (or not having it in the model sould increase it by an order of magnitude), which makes me suspect that there may be something fundamentally wrong with my setup? Any suggestions on how to proceed to diagnose, what's going on here? I'm really not making any progress here with fixing this alone unfortunately.

Best,
Vincent

Hi Vincent,

Sorry to drag up this topic after so long, but I was wondering whether you were able to resolve this issue? I'm working on an analysis that is at a similar scale (basically the contiguous US) and I'm having a similar problem where the range value can be several thousand kilometers, and for some models it is estimated at a few hundred kilometers. I've also had the same model produce a different range value (hundreds to thousands of km) each time I run the model.

Any insights you have would be much appreciated.

Thanks,

Jay

On Tuesday, December 10, 2019 at 4:57:05 PM UTC-7, Vincent von Dosky wrote:

Just a short follow up, in case this rings a bell for anyone.

I am still unable to fully make sense of the output of my hyperparameters. But in another model I was able to resolve the issue with the range, but at the cost of having another hyperparameter with way of the normal range :

Meanwhile I've done the model selection for another response (inverse Simpson index) from the same data-set (same mesh, same prior median range, but slightly different sd for the SPDE and not a poisson, but gaussian model).
There, the best fitting model (f1 below) has the spatio-temporal term, too (like the best fitting model for species richness). But, judging by DIC & WAIC the best model for inverse Simpson included a temporal random effect and a temporal autocorrelated effect. In f1, the issue with the huge range that I had with the model for species richness is gone - I have a range which makes somewhat sense. However, now the precision of the for my temporal random term is extremely high.

Out of curiosity, I also made a model including the effects for the best model for species richness (f2 below) so this model contains only the effects of the model in the previous emails (spatio-temporal effect and iid effect) - there the huge range for the spatial random effect is suddenly back to what it was in the other model.

I find this odd, as I would not expect that adding another separable temporal term should be able to reduce the range of the spatial correlation so much (or not having it in the model sould increase it by an order of magnitude), which makes me suspect that there may be something fundamentally wrong with my setup? Any suggestions on how to proceed to diagnose, what's going on here? I'm really not making any progress here with fixing this alone unfortunately.

Best,
Vincent

Hi Jason,

the common reasons for unclear identification of spatial correlation range parameters are that 1) from a single realisation the parameter isn't necessarily identifiable, and 2) when the identification isn't clear (e.g. the data are consistent with both a long range (when covariates don't capture all the large scale structure) and a short range (when the covariates don't capture all the small scale structure)
In these cases, the prior distribution chosen for the parameters becomes very important; if the random field is meant to capture large scale phenomena, the prior needs to reflect that, and to capture smaller scale phenomena, it needs to reflect that. If there aren't enough other components in the model, then you might even need two separate random field components, that can each capture either small or large scales (and separated by the choices of priors).

For the non- or weakly- identified models, the estimation is also more sensitive to numerical computation issues.

Finn
